snip.t: Delayed afterdepolarizations (DADs) $\rightarrow$ Intracellular calcium overload (e.g., digoxin toxicity, catecholamine excess) $\rightarrow$ Spontaneous calcium release $\rightarrow$ Cell depolarizes after full repolarization $\rightarrow$ Ventricular tachycardia.
*Rate:* Bradycardia (<60 bpm) seen in sinus node dysfunction, AV nodal blocks, or digoxin toxicity; tachycardia (>100 bpm) in SVT, VT, AF.
Hyperkalaemia: Stop ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone; renal replacement — Serial ECGs, glucose, renal profile — Digoxin toxicity (calcium caution); never give IV push K+

qs.q: Which electrolyte imbalance potentiates digoxin toxicity?
qs.e: Potassium (K⁺) and digoxin compete for binding sites on the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Hypokalemia leads to increased digoxin binding and toxicity, even at therapeutic levels. Hyperkalemia offers some protection.

qs.e: Hypokalemia increases digoxin binding to Na/K-ATPase, worsening toxicity.

o: Tachycardia and hypertension as early signs
Xanthopsia (yellow vision), nausea, bradycardia, heart block, and ventricular arrhythmias
qs.e: Digoxin toxicity features: GI (nausea, vomiting, anorexia), CNS (xanthopsia — yellow-green visual disturbance, confusion), cardiac (bradycardia, AV block, ventricular arrhythmias — PAT with block is classic). Hypokalemia WORSENS toxicity (K+ and digoxin compete for same Na/K ATPase binding site). Therapeutic range: 0.5–2.0 ng/mL.
